READING GUIDE
Scope and source notes
LeetCode metadata. Numbers, official titles, URL slugs, difficulty, and Premium flags use the official catalog
retrieved on 13 October 2026. The merge checked the workbook header ID against its embedded practice-link slug
for all 329 entries.
Deduplication. One master record is retained per LeetCode ID. All 273 overlaps now carry both their LinkedIn
references and the workbook page reference. The directory is an index, so its links do not create extra practice
entries.
General exercises. The 47 earlier exercises without a confirmed exact LeetCode match remain in a separate
section. Related LeetCode problems can impose different inputs, outputs, or constraints; those differences are
retained. No guessed ID was assigned.
Workbook text. The source workbook describes independent task restatements and empty JavaScript starters. Its
constraints, examples, N/B/G list badges, and historical verification caveats are preserved; they were not
independently revalidated during this merge. Current judge details are available through each official problem link.
Source verification caveat. The uploaded workbook reports that its 59 added entries used public reference
snapshots, rather than independently confirmed live LeetCode content. Its Premium limits are likewise not
confirmed against the current Premium judge. These statements belong to the supplied workbook, not to a new
verification of its examples or limits.
Page numbers. The directory shows physical page numbers in this merged PDF. Retained practice pages also
receive a small merged-page footer; any existing workbook page number printed above it refers to the original
uploaded workbook.
Source labels. S01-S45 identify the LinkedIn posts in the source directory. P01 identifies the uploaded workbook.
Titles link to LeetCode; the workbook-page column links to a retained practice page when one exists.
Catalog: Official LeetCode problem catalog

Problem statement
For each index i, return the product of every value in nums except nums[i]. The result must have

space apart from the returned array.
Input & expected result
Return a new array of products. Excluding an element means excluding that particular index, not
every occurrence of the same value. Handle zeros directly; dividing a total product is not allowed.
EXAMPLE 1
Input: nums = [2,3,0,4]
Output: [0,0,24,0]
Explanation: Only the position containing zero has a nonzero answer: the other values multiply
to 24. Every other product includes the zero.
EXAMPLE 2
Input: nums = [0,2,0]
Output: [0,0,0]
Explanation: Removing any single position still leaves at least one zero in the product.

• nums[i]: -30 through 30 (inclusive)

Problem statement
nums contains n + 1 integers, each between 1 and n. Exactly one distinct value appears more than
once; it may appear more than twice. Return that repeated value. Do not alter nums, and use
constant extra space. Seek a solution with linear running time.
Input & expected result

allowed values. Return the duplicate value regardless of its occurrence count. Sorting or marking

findMedian() returns the middle value of the sorted data for an odd count, or the mean of the
middle two for an even count. It is called only after at least one insertion. The constructor begins

value 6.

Explanation: The two sorted values have arithmetic mean (-2 + 3) / 2 = 0.5.

adds an absent value and reports true, or returns false if it already exists. remove(val) deletes a

Problem statement
Implement TimeMap. set(key,value,timestamp) records a value at that time. get(key,timestamp)
returns the value recorded for that key at the greatest stored time no later than the requested
time, or "" if none exists. set timestamps are strictly increasing across calls. The constructor
creates an empty store.
Input & expected result
Different keys maintain independent histories. A lookup may ask about a time between updates,
before the first update, or after the last update. get does not add a record and must return an
empty string when no qualifying history exists.
EXAMPLE 1
Operations: set("a","old",2), set("a","new",5), get("a",4), get("a",5)
Query results: "old", "new"
Explanation: Time 4 uses the earlier record at time 2; time 5 includes the update made exactly
at that timestamp.
EXAMPLE 2
Operations: set("x","v",5), get("x",4), get("x",9), get("y",9)
Query results: "", "v", ""
Explanation: No x record exists by time 4, the time-5 record remains valid at time 9, and y has
no history.
Constraints & guarantees
• key.length, value.length: 1 through 100 (inclusive)
• timestamp: 1 through 10^7 (inclusive)
• Keys and values use a-z and digits. set timestamps increase strictly across calls. Combined method
calls: at most 2 * 10^5

Problem statement
Implement DetectSquares. add(point) stores one occurrence of an integer coordinate pair; identical
points count as separate occurrences. count(point) returns how many ways three stored
occurrences and the query point can form a square of positive area whose sides are parallel to the
coordinate axes. The query need not be stored and is not automatically added.
Input & expected result
Only axis-aligned squares with nonzero side length qualify. Stored multiplicities multiply the
number of available choices for the other three corners. The query point supplies one corner
regardless of whether that coordinate has previously been added.
EXAMPLE 1
Add [1,1], [1,3], [3,1]; count([3,3]) returns 1.
Add [1,1] again; count([3,3]) now returns 2.
Explanation: The three stored coordinates complete one square with [3,3]. Duplicating [1,1]
creates a second choice for that corner and doubles the count.
EXAMPLE 2
Add [0,0], [0,2], [3,0]; count([3,2])
Output: 0
Explanation: These corners form a 3-by-2 rectangle, not a square.
Constraints & guarantees
• point.length == 2
• x, y: 0 through 1000 (inclusive)
• Combined add/count calls: at most 3000
